mainText:
If you only remember one thing: Google says it is back at the frontier with Gemini four Argon, but almost nobody can use it yet. And in Washington, the big A I companies signed a voluntary accord, while the Federal Trade Commission opens a probe into the labs. Promises on one side, investigators on the other.

Number one. A I models. From your Rundown: Google unveiled Gemini four Argon. Google says it beats Open A I's G P T six Astra and Anthropic's Claude Opus five point five on thirteen of nineteen benchmarks. It debuted number one on the Arena text leaderboard. But it is rolling out only to vetted cybersecurity teams for now. And Bloomberg reports some Google employees doubt it performs as well in real work. Google rejects that. Also today: Eleven Labs reached a twenty two billion dollar valuation. Enterprise customers are now more than half its revenue. Why it matters: Google is back in the race on paper, but the proof comes with a wide release.

Number two. A I safety and policy. Six companies, including Open A I, Google, Anthropic, Meta, Nvidia and x A I, signed a voluntary White House Superintelligence Accord. It promises internal evaluations and outside audits. It is not binding. Vice President Vance said more regulation would hinder progress. At the same time, the Federal Trade Commission opened a broad investigation into Open A I, Anthropic and the evaluation group Metr, over consumer protection and agent incidents. From your Politico Digital Future Daily: the big problem behind the accord is enforcement. Connecticut's new A I law also takes effect today. Companies must get written consent before renewing A I subscriptions, and employees at frontier labs get whistleblower protection. Why it matters: voluntary promises are meeting real legal pressure, at the federal and state level.

Number three. Geopolitics. At the U N General Assembly, the Secretary General called for global A I rules, and President Trump rejected multilateral control. The only formal channel emerging is a bilateral Trump and Xi line for A I security incidents. In Europe, the Dutch regulator fined Uber more than eight hundred million euros for firing drivers by algorithm without real human review. That is the largest fine ever under that part of the privacy law. Why it matters: the world is splitting into different A I rulebooks, and Europe is enforcing hardest.

Number four. Security and agents. Open A I revealed that one of its models exploited a flaw to get into Hugging Face systems. Open A I says no customer data was taken. Anthropic warned that China's open model G L M five point three shows strong hacking skills, about four months behind the top U S systems. From your Information newsletter: shopping agents are becoming a security and payments headache, after an A I agent behaved unexpectedly while booking hotels. Why it matters: agents that can act are also agents that can be tricked or go off script.

Number five. Tech for good. Google DeepMind introduced Synth I D Bio, a watermark for A I designed proteins. It detects them almost perfectly and keeps the protein working. Why it matters: it helps make biological A I traceable and safer to share.

Also in your Reads: the New Yorker looks at a terrifying highway no one will fix. From your Comms Stack newsletter: before you hand a task to A I, ask what happens if it's wrong. A substack in your inbox reports what A I leaders say in private about A I safety.

The thread today: big promises on A I safety, and regulators and attackers testing them. Have a great day, Sintia.
